blocks.text: Every child in Turkey knows *Keloğlan*, the bald boy: *kel* (bald) + *oğlan* (boy). He is poor, usually lives alone with his mother, and looks like nobody's idea of a hero: a bit clumsy, a bit lazy, sometimes naive. Yet in tale after tale he outwits giants (*dev*), greedy merchants and proud sultans, often with nothing but a quick answer and some luck, and at the end he may well marry the sultan's daughter.
Heroes like him turn up across the Turkic world, as *Keçel* in Azerbaijan or *Tazoğlan* in Crimea, and folklorists have compared him with the humble youth who wins the princess in European tales.

A Turkish tale doesn't open with **once upon a time** but with a *tekerleme*, a playful rhyming formula. The best known is *Bir varmış, bir yokmuş* (Once there was, once there wasn't). Another tells the listener that the story belongs to no real time or place:

blocks.tr: Evvel zaman içinde, kalbur saman içinde…
blocks.en: Long, long ago, when the sieve was in the straw…
blocks.source: Traditional opening of Turkish folk tales

blocks.text: The endings are just as fixed. *Onlar ermiş muradına, biz çıkalım kerevetine* (They got their heart's desire; now let's climb onto our divan) sends everyone back to real life. Another closing has three apples fall from the sky, *gökten üç elma düştü*: one for the storyteller, one for the listener, and the third, depending on the version, for the teller again or for whoever takes the tale's lesson to heart.

For centuries tales were passed on by word of mouth, very often told by women to children. Among the first to write them down from storytellers was the Hungarian Turkologist Ignác Kúnos, who arrived in Istanbul in 1885 and travelled in Anatolia. His collections came out from 1889, in English as Turkish Fairy Tales and Folk Tales (London, 1896) and Forty-four Turkish Fairy Tales (1913). In 1953 the folklorist Pertev Naili Boratav and the German scholar Wolfram Eberhard published a catalogue that sorted the recorded Turkish tales by plot type.
Keloğlan has since moved to the cinema, the stage and children's television, most recently in the cartoon series *Keloğlan Masalları*.
Listen to the verbs: tales are told with `-mIş`, the form of this unit for things the speaker didn't witness. Here is how a Keloğlan tale might begin:

blocks.tr: Bir varmış, bir yokmuş. Bir köyde fakir bir kadın ve oğlu varmış. Oğlanın saçı yokmuş, ama çok akıllıymış. Adı Keloğlan'mış. Bir gün Keloğlan şehre gitmiş. Orada padişahın çok güzel bir kızı varmış.
blocks.en: Once there was, once there wasn't. In a village there lived a poor woman and her son. The boy had no hair, but he was very clever. His name was Keloğlan. One day Keloğlan went to the city. There the sultan had a very beautiful daughter.

vocab.en: rhyming formula that opens or closes a tale

questions.q: Why does the tale say *varmış* and *gitmiş*, not *vardı* and *gitti*?
options: The storyteller didn't see it happen
questions.explain: `-mIş` is for what the speaker didn't witness: the voice of tales and jokes.
